## What Is an Employer of Record in Rwanda


An Employer of Record (EOR) is a third-party company that becomes the legal employer of your workers in a foreign country. The EOR handles employment contracts, payroll processing, tax withholdings, and statutory benefits, while you retain day-to-day control over what your team members actually do.


In Rwanda's context, this matters a great deal. To hire someone in Rwanda without an EOR, you'd typically need to register a local legal entity, register with the Rwanda Revenue Authority (RRA), and comply with the Labour Law and social security obligations under the Rwanda Social Security Board (RSSB). That process takes months and carries ongoing administrative overhead.


An EOR removes that requirement entirely. Your hire gets onboarded under the EOR's existing legal structure in Rwanda, and you get a worker ready to contribute without setting up a subsidiary.


### Why Companies Use an EOR in Rwanda


- Hiring is faster: you can bring on Rwanda-based talent in days instead of waiting months for entity registration to clear. For a broader look at[EOR international hiring and expansion](https://www.bolto.com/blog/eor-international-global-hiring-expansion-guide) , the strategies apply across markets.
- Compliance is handled locally: the EOR knows Rwandan labor law, statutory contribution rates, and required benefits, so your team members are covered correctly from day one.
- Risk is reduced: the EOR takes on primary responsibility for local compliance, which can limit your exposure to misclassification and non-compliance penalties when you work within the agreement's scope. This is not a guarantee of any legal or regulatory outcome.
- You stay flexible: if your Rwanda hiring needs change, winding down is far simpler than dissolving a legal entity.


## Employment Laws and Compliance Requirements in Rwanda


Rwanda's labor framework is governed by the[Rwanda Labour Code](https://antislaverylaw.ac.uk/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/Rwanda-Labour-Law.pdf) , which sets the foundational rules for employment contracts, working hours, termination, and worker protections. If you're hiring in Rwanda, here's what you need to know.


### Contracts and Working Hours


Employment contracts in Rwanda can be fixed-term or indefinite, and they must be written in a language the employee understands. The standard workweek is 40 hours, and overtime is generally compensated at a premium rate above regular pay (MIFOTRA Ministerial Order No. 01/MIFOTRA/23, 2023).


### Leave Entitlements


- Employees are entitled to paid annual leave after 12 months of continuous service, with the number of days set by Ministerial Order under Rwanda's Labour Law.
- Maternity leave entitlements and conditions are set by Ministerial Order under Rwanda's Labour Law. Rwanda law also prohibits employers from terminating a pregnant employee's contract on the basis of pregnancy (Law n° 027/2023, Article 24 bis).
- Sick leave entitlements vary based on length of service and medical certification requirements.


### Termination and Notice Periods


Termination rules under the Labour Code require valid grounds and appropriate notice periods, which generally scale with the employee's length of service. Wrongful dismissal can expose a company to serious liability, so documentation matters.


### Social Security and Tax Obligations


Employers are generally required to register employees with the[Rwanda Social Security Board (RSSB)](https://www.rssb.rw/scheme/pension-scheme) and contribute to pension and medical insurance schemes. As of 2026, the RSSB pension scheme requires a 6% employer contribution and a 6% employee contribution (RSSB & RRA, 2026). Personal income tax rates are progressive, reaching up to 30% for higher earners (RRA, 2026).


Obligation Details


RSSB Pension Contribution Employer: 6%, Employee: 6% (as of 2026; RSSB & RRA, 2026)


Medical Insurance 7.5% employer, 7.5% employee; 15% of basic salary (RSSB, 2026)


Income Tax (top rate) 30% (RRA, 2026)


Standard Workweek 40 hours (MIFOTRA Ministerial Order No. 01/MIFOTRA/23, 2023)


This is general information, not legal advice. Rules vary by situation and change over time, so consult a qualified employment lawyer for your specific circumstances.

## Cost of Hiring in Rwanda with an EOR vs. a Local Entity


Hiring in Rwanda through a local entity versus an Employer of Record involves a real cost trade-off that's worth thinking through carefully before you commit to either path.


Setting up a legal entity in Rwanda typically requires registration fees, a local legal team, an accountant, and ongoing administrative overhead. Many companies spend several months and tens of thousands of dollars getting through entity setup alone, before a single employee is paid. Once the entity is running, you're responsible for maintaining compliance with the Rwanda Revenue Authority, filing payroll taxes, and managing statutory contributions on your own.


An EOR removes that upfront burden. You pay a monthly service fee per employee, and the EOR handles payroll, tax filings, and statutory benefits on your behalf. General industry EOR fees typically range from $300 to $1,000 per employee per month, though the exact cost depends on the provider and scope of service. Reviewing the[best EOR companies for global hiring](https://www.bolto.com/blog/best-eor-companies-global-hiring-guide) can help you compare what different providers cover. These figures are not Bolto's pricing.


Here's a rough cost comparison to frame the decision: setup time for a local entity runs 2 to 6 months and carries high upfront costs (legal, notary, capital), while an EOR is ready in days with no registration fees. Ongoing compliance management is handled in-house or by local advisors with an entity, but is included in the EOR service fee. Payroll tax filing is self-managed with an entity and managed by the EOR otherwise. A local entity typically requires 15 or more employees to make the economics work; an EOR is practical for just 1 to 2 hires.


For companies hiring one to five employees in Rwanda, an EOR is generally the more cost-effective path. Consulting a[global employer of record provider guide](https://www.bolto.com/blog/global-employer-of-record-provider-guide) can help you weigh those trade-offs before committing. Local entity setup makes more sense when you're building a larger, permanent team and can spread those fixed costs across enough headcount to support them.


*This is general information, not legal or financial advice. Costs and requirements vary by situation and change over time. Consult a qualified employment lawyer or financial advisor for guidance specific to your circumstances.*

## EOR vs. Local Entity in Rwanda: Which Is Right for You


When you want to hire in Rwanda, you have two real paths: set up a local legal entity or work through an Employer of Record (EOR). Each has its place, and the right choice depends on your timeline, budget, and hiring volume.


Setting up a Rwandan entity gives you direct control and can make sense if you plan to hire 15 or more people in-country over the long term. Tech companies in particular may find value in reviewing[EOR software for tech startups](https://www.bolto.com/blog/best-eor-softwares-for-tech-startups) before selecting a platform. The trade-off is real: registration through the Rwanda Development Board typically takes several weeks, and you will still need local legal counsel, a registered office location, and the bandwidth to manage ongoing compliance with the Rwanda Revenue Authority and Rwanda Social Security Board (RSSB).


An EOR skips that setup entirely. Your hire is onboarded under the EOR's existing legal entity in Rwanda, so you can have someone working in days instead of months.


Here is a quick comparison to help you decide: a local entity takes several weeks to months to stand up and carries high upfront costs for legal, registration, and office setup, but gives you low ongoing compliance burden managed internally and works best for large, committed headcount where flexibility to exit is low. An EOR, by contrast, is ready in days, costs little upfront, keeps compliance managed by the EOR, and offers high flexibility to exit, making it the right fit when you're testing a market or hiring a small team.


For most companies hiring one to five people in Rwanda, an EOR is the faster and lower-risk path. If your Rwanda headcount grows and the market proves out, converting to a local entity later remains an option.

## FAQs


### How does an employer of record in Rwanda compare to setting up a local entity?


An EOR lets you hire in Rwanda in days, skipping the months of entity registration, and works best for teams of one to five people. A local entity gives you more direct control and lower per-employee costs at scale, but only makes financial sense once you have enough headcount (typically 15 or more) to spread the setup and ongoing compliance costs.


### What does Bolto's employer of record service cover for Rwanda-based hires?


Bolto handles the full employment lifecycle: compliant contracts under Rwanda's Labour Code, payroll in Rwandan francs with PAYE withholding, RSSB pension and medical contributions, statutory benefits, and ongoing HR support including leave management and offboarding. New hires can be onboarded in as little as 48 hours.


### Can I hire in Rwanda without registering a legal entity or dealing with the Rwanda Revenue Authority myself?


Yes. Through an EOR, your hire works under the EOR's existing legal entity in Rwanda, so you never need to register with the Rwanda Development Board, maintain a local office location, or manage direct filings with the Rwanda Revenue Authority. The EOR handles those obligations on your behalf.


### What are the employer of record Rwanda RSSB contribution rates I should budget for?


Under Rwanda's social security framework as of 2026, the employer contribution to the RSSB pension scheme is 6% and the employee contribution is 6% (RSSB & RRA, 2026). This rate applies through 2026, with planned annual increases starting in 2027 toward a combined 20% rate by 2030. Separate employer and employee contributions of 7.5% each are required for medical insurance, totaling 15% of basic salary (RSSB, 2026). These figures reflect the general requirements under Rwandan law and may change, so confirm current rates with a qualified employment adviser before finalizing your budget.


### When does it make sense to move from an EOR in Rwanda to a local entity?


An EOR makes more sense when you are testing the Rwanda market or hiring a small team. If your Rwanda headcount grows to 15 or more people and the market has proven out, the fixed costs of a local entity start to spread across enough employees to support the setup investment, at which point converting becomes worth considering.
